At first glance, the humpback chub doesn’t look as if it could determine the future of nations. Its lower body is par for the fishy course: a pearlescent ombré going from green to gray, its trunk girthy, its tail tapering and lithe. But the chub’s head seems borrowed from another fish entirely, with a grumpy, vaguely prehistoric face under the bony hump that gives the species its name. For the last 3.5 million years, the humpback chub has evolved to live in one place alone: the turbid tributaries and main stem of the Colorado River in the Southwestern United States. Its eyes are made for piercing muddy waters, its mouth and gills for sifting out sediment. Young chub shelter in shoreline eddies, while adults frequent deep canyon pools near rapids. Chub eat whatever the river gives them: insects, crustaceans, plants, seeds, and one another. Most never leave the ten-mile stretch of river they were born in and develop borderline-monogamous relationships with a particular rock or riffle in their range. Some can live as long as forty years and grow to twenty inches in length. In spring, when the river can reach a relatively balmy sixty degrees, the fins of the mature chub flush a startling red: It’s spawning season. As for the much-ballyhooed hump, scientists are divided. Some think that it helps the chub stay right side up in the mythic cataracts of the Grand Canyon; others, that it protects them from predators. But it doesn’t matter who’s right. The point is that the humpback chub is functional but a bit of an uggo. And yet, despite its unprepossessing mien, the fish has inspired decades of passionate admirers and detractors, a whole host of partisans willing to either kill it or kill for it.

The humpback chub was one of the last large fish species discovered in North America, after prospectors and settlers pulled them out of the Grand Canyon’s Bright Angel Creek in 1933. Americans began engineering their extinction almost immediately. The Hoover Dam, completed a few years later, wiped out the lower Grand Canyon population. Up the river in northern Utah, Flaming Gorge Dam and years of wholesale poisoning designed to replace the chub with a trout fishery nearly wiped out another. And in 1963 the federal government completed Glen Canyon Dam, the massive concrete wall just upstream of the Grand Canyon, and transformed the Colorado River from a warm, muddy, flood-prone system into a cold, clear, tightly regulated channel hospitable to nonnative sport fish and much more hostile to the chub. The dam also created Lake Powell, a giant reservoir built for water storage, hydropower, bass fishing, and huge houseboats. The government stocked the reservoir above the dam with nonnative smallmouth bass and the new tailwater below the dam with trout. Native fish like the humpback chub were regarded as primitive holdovers to be replaced by more desirable species. By the late 1960s, the chub’s numbers were so reduced that it landed itself the dubious distinction of being on the first endangered species list. Not that it did much good. By the 1990s, the chub was gasping its last breath, with just 3,500 swimmers left below the dam.

In 1992, Congress, suddenly aware of the dam’s consequences on ecosystems, cultural sites, and native fish downstream, passed the Grand Canyon Protection Act to conserve its ecological resources while also preserving the primacy of water delivery and hydropower, a contradiction that has defined the river ever since. Federal management is now overseen by an acronym-studded bureaucracy that tasks twenty-seven stakeholders—six tribes, the seven states that rely on the river, hydropower officials, scientists, fishermen, environmentalists, and water managers—with collecting data, running conservation experiments, releasing sediment to rebuild eroded beaches, and ensuring hydropower and water delivery, among other, often conflicting, priorities.

Thanks to these interventions, the chub is recovering. Federal agencies estimate that more than eleven thousand of them now live in the tributaries of the Little Colorado River, with as many as 120,000 thriving in the western Grand Canyon near Lake Mead. The chub’s humble, humped existence—and the fight over its future—has inspired one of the largest, most vociferous conservation debates of the twenty-first century: What should a river be, and for whom? Everyone seems to have an answer. There are the restorationists, who want to bring back something resembling the old river: warm water, seasonal floods, sediment, native fish. There are the pragmatists, who believe the dam is here to stay and the task must be managing its artificial ecosystem. Then there are the trout guides furious that a beloved fishery and recreation economy are being sacrificed, the tribal leaders questioning whether controlling the river was ever legitimate, and the agencies, operators, farmers, and cities whose survival depends on the dam. As rising temperatures and decades of overuse drive water levels in Lake Powell and Lake Mead toward all-time lows, the Southwest’s future is increasingly entangled with the fate of a fish most people have never heard of.

I suppose now is a good time to tell you that I have never seen the humpback chub in the flesh. It’s not for lack of trying. Over the past two years, I have rafted almost the entire 1,450 miles of the Colorado River, from Wyoming to the Gulf of California in Mexico, hoping to understand the ramifications of an American West built atop the fantasy of infinite water in a desert. I have seen the graveyards of the Cataract Canyon, where Lake Powell has drowned miles of the river’s notorious rapids; I have seen the waters of Lake Mead so low that treasure hunters scan the mudflats with metal detectors; and I have seen the delta where the Colorado meets the Gulf of California, formerly one of the most biologically diverse places in North America, reduced to miles of sand. On most of these stretches of river, the chub is barely hanging on, and sightings are rare.

It’s not for lack of trying that I have never seen the humpback chub in the flesh.

While paddling, I often thought about the conspicuous absence of the chub beneath the waters and what it means about what we humans have done above. I knew the fish were most plentiful in the Grand Canyon, so I did my damnedest to get a glimpse of the chub there. I invited myself on an electrofishing trip that fell through; applied to join conversation research trips where the scientists, afraid of angering the Trump regime and getting DOGE’d out of existence, decided they didn’t want a reporter tagging along; and considered prohibitively expensive commercial trips. I finally got on a trip through the National Park Service, but staffing cuts scuttled it, and I was switched to another trip, until a forest fire came along and burned parts of the park to ashes. All the while, the true determinant of the river’s fate remained stubbornly out of reach, hidden behind bureaucracy, secreted in its deep canyon pools beneath rapids and boulders.

I have compensated for the chub’s absence with digital comforts. On any given night, I have watched YouTube videos of scientists wading into muddy tributaries, throwing out hoop nets baited with cheese. The chub come up gulping, their skin nearly translucent in the sudden light. The scientists lay the chub on measuring boards. They palpate a spot near the head and declare them male or female. They move deliberately, returning the fish to buckets with a surreal calm in the face of prolonged distress. I once read that a fish’s sense of time is not like ours: When it is pulled from the depths, it experiences this as a perpetual, terrifying ascent, and when it lands on the beach, it is forever. On other nights, I have added myself to the almost 180 YouTubers who have watched a team of biologists helicopter into the Grand Canyon and release three hundred chub—netted the year before and raised over the winter at a hatchery—back into Shinumo Creek. I read about electrofishing expeditions in the river, where researchers send electric currents into the water, and fish rise, stunned, belly up, into waiting nets. If the chub aren’t already tagged, the researchers slide a hollow needle into their bodies to implant a tracker or a brightly colored mark. One scientist joked that this amounts to abduction, imagining one of his fish returning to its companions to describe a higher power that came without warning, probed it, and released it back into the river. I find it impossible not to sympathize with the creature.

Not everyone shares my particular obsession with this elusive, ugly fish. But the chub’s continued existence is bound up with the survival of the long-imperiled Colorado River. For five million years, the Colorado flowed relatively unmolested from the Rocky Mountains to the Gulf of California. But in 1922, a group of politicians, engineers, lawyers, and land speculators led by then–Secretary of Commerce Herbert Hoover gathered at a resort just outside Santa Fe to divide the Colorado River between the upper basin states of Utah, Colorado, Wyoming, and New Mexico and the lower basin states of California, Arizona, and Nevada.

These captains of industry wanted to build cities in the desert and agricultural empires under the scorching sun. And to do that, they needed water. More accurately, they needed to believe that the water they needed was there in abundance. And so, in a rare wet year, they chose to believe that the river carried far more water than it actually did and parceled out more than the Colorado could reliably provide in a fit of wishful thinking. The resulting Colorado River Compact required the upper basin states to not deplete the downstream flow below a certain quantity—a promise made possible by massive dams, like Glen Canyon, that store wet years against dry ones, distribute water deliveries to thirsty states, and generate enough hydropower to keep the lights on for millions of people across the Southwest. Desert cities became major metropolises, and the Southwest, an agricultural powerhouse dependent on the water and power provided by the river, necessarily bought into the delusion that the river could support endless growth. Forty million people from Denver to Los Angeles now depend on this mistake. So do the five hundred thousand acres of farmland in the Imperial Valley, which is why we have salads in the wintertime and ice cream in the summer. Meanwhile, the dam managers, hydropower interests, and state water negotiators who control and allocate the river have become some of the most powerful players in the West.

Because of the aforementioned permitting issues, forest fires, and government shutdowns, it took me three years to join Dave Foster aboard a small metal skiff below the Glen Canyon Dam, fifteen miles of placid river before the rapids begin in terrifying earnest. “We have the ability to alter our environment, and we’ve done it because you make those changes in order to live a certain way,” said Foster, a veteran trout fisherman and trout guide in the tailwaters below the dam. “And there are repercussions.” Climate change is currently finishing the job overallocation started. Things are so bad that, before the end of the year, the reservoir could reach what is known as “dead pool” levels. At this point, hydropower would fail, and no water could be sent downstream. One of the country’s most important rivers would be reduced to a trickle, taps would run dry, and the entire economy of the Southwest would grind to a halt. Foster has seen these impacts firsthand: He’s taken thousands of families down the river in the blue-ribbon fishery just below the dam, teaching them both skills (like casting) and virtues (like patience).

From where we sat, the dam rose in a curve above our heads, durable enough to hold back the flexing muscle of an entire river. Telephone poles and electrical wires cross willy-nilly on the cliffside, carrying electricity generated by the dam’s penstocks to the people. When Foster was a little kid, a person could drive all the way to the base of the dam and put their hand on it, feeling the warmth of all the mechanical energy thrumming inside. Now that’s impossible. Where we sat, we could see signs admonishing us to keep out and stay back, as well as the guard towers. When Foster was running logistics for the Grand Canyon Monitoring and Research Center, he took an electrofishing boat up here one night to do some tagging and found himself surrounded by armed guards with machine guns. “There’s guys watching us right now,” he said.

This pageantry is deliberate and, in the eyes of the state, utterly necessary. Since its erection in 1963, this giant wedge of concrete has been one of the most contested inanimate objects in the country, right up there with Mount Rushmore. Cowboy anarchists and river runners waged a yearslong direct action campaign to take it down. The radical environmentalist group Earth First! dropped a giant banner that resembled a crack down its surface. And Utah’s most iconic and controversial environmentalist misanthrope, Edward Abbey, wrote a novel about blowing it up.

Foster told us that the Colorado used to be so muddy that settlers joked that it was too thin to plow and too thick to drink. But that was not the river we passed over as we motored up the canyon toward the dam. There, the waters were crystal clear, and there were shadows of fish and ripples where they jumped. All around us, red sandstone walls rose up, ancient and majestic. At one point, Foster pointed out a nest on top of an electric pole. “Osprey,” he said. But the air was otherwise woefully underwinged. There were few birds there because there were few bugs. Unaware of the timetables of industry, bugs lay their hatches in the low waters; but when hydropower demand surges, the water does too, sweeping the hatch away.

Foster stopped the boat, and we idled, taking in the silence. I peered into the water. Once, humpback chub congregated here so thickly that you could practically walk across the water on their backs. But when the dam went up in 1963, the whole ecosystem changed. “There were seven native fish species,” Foster said, “and one of three things happened. Either they dealt with the changed environment and thrived, which would be the case with the flannelmouth sucker. Or they went completely extinct almost immediately, which would be the case of the Colorado pikeminnow. Or they were somewhere in between—that would be the humpback chub.” The cold, clear water coming from the base of the dam was a death warrant for the chub, which loves its water muddy and warm. As the reservoir began to fill, the government stocked it with nonnative bass, and the tailwaters below with trout of all stripes, flying planes over the water and dumping their cargo from hundreds of feet. “There is a stretch of this river that is uninhabitable by humpback chub because of the dam,” Foster told me. But the engineered conditions below the dam were nearly perfect for rainbow trout. For a time, the fishery was one of the river’s official management priorities. But after an ecologist observed government workers poisoning chub habitats with rotenone to make room for nonnative fish like trout—turning the river an unnerving, Egyptian-plague red—he wrote an op-ed for the New York Times decrying the practice. The article landed on the desk of Wallace Stegner, who, outraged, called then–Interior Secretary Stewart Udall. The furor led to the creation of the endangered species list.

After that, everything changed. Money poured in to protect the chub and a legion of advocates stood ready to sue in its name. Before the Grand Canyon Protection Act, Foster explained, Glen Canyon Dam was operated almost entirely for hydropower demand: River flows could surge from three thousand cubic feet per second to twenty thousand in a single day as electricity use rose and fell, creating what Foster described as an unnatural “daily tide” that dramatically eroded beaches and native fish habitat. But as the humpback chub became one of the causes célèbres of the newly created Glen Canyon Dam Adaptive Management Program, government agencies like the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Park Service engaged in increasingly elaborate interventions to protect it. Dam managers now release artificial floods to redistribute sediment, manipulate daily dam releases to reduce fluctuations in river height, and launch monitoring trips, electroshocking campaigns, fish counts, tagging operations, and predator-removal programs. The fish’s numbers have rebounded steadily enough; the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recently downgraded it from endangered to threatened. Ironically, part of that recovery has been aided by climate change itself, which has warmed the river downstream, creating better conditions for spawning. But this is a double-edged sword. As Lake Powell levels drop and its temperature rises, warmwater smallmouth bass—the same nonnative species the government had stocked in the reservoir just decades before—are getting sucked through the dam’s lower outlet tubes and into the river below. Smallmouth bass are aggressive, dominant, and voracious. Their favorite food? Humpback chub.

“Everybody flipped out,” Foster said. Officials began releasing colder water through bypass tubes located deeper in Lake Powell to suppress bass spawning downstream. Now it was the smallmouth bass’s turn to get electroshocked, netted, and poisoned. Foster pointed to the bank across the river: Earlier this year, he said, the Park Service spent roughly $1 million excavating a side channel there so colder water would circulate through it and eliminate nonnative intruders. Meanwhile, the chub might be regaining its finhold in some stretches of the river, but it still lacks the muddy, pre-dam waters it needs to thrive. And despite the government’s herculean efforts, more smallmouth bass are being spotted below the dam. If they establish themselves, then so long to the chub. And if the whole reservoir fails, as is increasingly likely, the river will cease flowing to cities and farms, which means it’s kaput for all involved.

This is the trap the dam has created: Every intervention solves one problem but creates another, and every action merely rearranges the casualties. One of the people tasked with managing the pandemonium is Larry Stevens, a zoologist who has spent more than fifty years studying the Colorado River. I encountered Stevens after clicking on a YouTube video titled “The Song of the Humpback Chub,” which turned out to be a jam, laying out the whole intractable debate around the fish chanted on top of a doo-wop-style backtrack. In multipart harmony, Stevens and his backup singers describe the water and hydropower barons exploiting the river, the scientists fighting for a piece of the chub research pie, and the government researchers who poke and prod the chub across a multitude of manufactured crises. The chub gets the refrain: “Bring back the river!” they plea. “Set that muddy water free!”

Artificially recreating a system that took millions of years to evolve is always sure to disappoint somebody.

Writing an entire song about the chub requires obsession, and Stevens is obsessed. After so many years working in the Glen Canyon, he’s about as deep in its bureaucracy as anyone can be. He sits on one of the two seats in the twenty-five-person Glen Canyon Dam Adaptive Management Work Group reserved for environmental advocates, as well as in the Technical Working Group, which meets twice a month to review the latest in conservation efforts and make management suggestions to the Department of the Interior, whose remit is to restore and enhance ecosystems downstream. In reality, Stevens said, “everybody is hammering their shoes on the table, saying, ‘I want more water for my agricultural constituents’ or ‘I want more stabilized flows for river running.’” There are very powerful lobbies at play. They may disagree on many things, but all of them must contend with the mandates of the Grand Canyon Protection Act, which means that they have to work together to save the native fish.

When I called him to talk chub, Stevens was frank. “My estimate is we’ve spent nearly half a billion dollars trying to save the humpback chub at this point.” And for all that money, Stevens said, we do not actually know why the chub are bouncing back. The system is too complex, he explained, and the interventions too extensive. But for Stevens, the effort is worth it. The Grand Canyon is one of the most iconic landscapes in the world, he said, and the world looks to it for leadership on conservation issues. The humpback chub is old enough to have survived ice age floods and battle-hardened enough to survive the dam. The fish, he explained, is what ecologists call an umbrella species. “If you protect that species, you’ll be protecting the habitat and all the other species in that habitat,” Stevens said. Bring back the chub, and you have to bring back the bugs, river flows, and temperatures it depends on. And once the chub returns, it could bring back the river otters and Colorado pikeminnow, which eat the chub. Save the chub, save the river. Save the river, save the world. Hard to put a price tag on that.

But saving an increasingly artificial river requires a lot of work. Stevens and his fellows in the dam bureaucracy monitor conditions, adjust flows, and rebuild habitats, then study the consequences and start all over again. Federal scientists electroshock stretches of the river to remove predatory bass, tag chub with implanted microchips, and then track their movements through the canyon with underwater scanners and radio telemetry. Managers keep the river cold enough to suppress warmwater predators but warm enough for native fish recruitment. Whole teams monitor sediment loads, spawning habitats, and side channels where baby fish might survive. Analysts sift through the data and argue over how to share it between the U.S. Geological Survey, the National Park Service, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Arizona Game and Fish Department, tribal governments, and the Bureau of Reclamation.

As threats from climate change mount and more interventions are required, managers have come to consider some truly wild ideas, like a giant “thermal curtain” that could selectively block warm surface water—and the larval bass drifting within it—from moving downstream. But the engineering know-how required would be so advanced that Stevens has pitched another idea, floated with the cheerful if slightly exhausted tone of a man who has spent decades trying to outwit a collapsing ecosystem: What if dam managers stocked the forebay above the dam with endangered Colorado pikeminnow, which would eat smallmouth bass before the bass made it through the outlet tubes and into chub habitats? A cyclical buffet for bottom feeders and seafood royalty alike. Like many of the scientists and managers who have spent decades inside the Adaptive Management Program, Stevens still believes that, with enough monitoring, engineering, and negotiation, the river’s contradictions can be balanced a little longer. The methodology may grow increasingly surreal—thermal curtains, artificial floods, endangered predator fish deployed like biological security guards—but the underlying faith remains the same: The chub can be saved.

Few people did more to build the system to save the chub than Jack Schmidt. Schmidt grew up on the East Coast, a river geomorphologist who didn’t lay an oar in the Grand Canyon until 1981, when he rafted it with friends. For weeks, they maneuvered their rubber crafts through the froth by day and drank cheap beer on the beaches by night. One night midway through the trip, drunk on canyon grandeur and Milwaukee’s Best, he proposed a pact: Permits be damned, let’s stay here forever.

It’s an institutionalized river, shaped less by nature than by rules.

In the 1990s, Schmidt helped push for the legislation that established the Grand Canyon Monitoring and Research Center and, in 2011, became an administrator. His teams conduct sediment studies, flow experiments, fish counts, and temperature models. In the morning he might authorize electrofishing expeditions, on his lunch break worry over water temperatures, and on his drive home wonder how long before both the dams dry up, break down, or fill with mud. All day he is tasked with playing God, and every night he ends up as somebody’s devil because artificially recreating a system that took millions of years to evolve is always sure to disappoint somebody. But after decades inside the machinery, Schmidt has arrived at a dark conclusion. “We’ve got enough science that we can make the Grand Canyon whatever you want,” he told me. “The problem is we don’t know what we want.”

When I met Schmidt in Logan, Utah, at his home—a low sprawl of wooden buildings connected by outdoor walkways—his office was covered in river maps, the corners of which were held down with piles of sandstone rocks. When I asked him how the river had changed since the dam was built, he paused. “It’s really blue and green,” he said. “And it used to be red and brown.” Before Glen Canyon Dam went up in the 1960s, the Colorado carried an enormous sediment load, whisking red rock downstream in great muddy pulses. Spring runoff scoured the canyon clean, uprooting vegetation. The river was warm, silty, and violent. Then the dam flipped everything. It trapped sediment behind the reservoir, slowly filling Lake Powell with mud while starving the river downstream. Dam managers implemented a flow regime based on electricity demand. Penstocks pulled cold water from deep in Lake Powell and replaced the warm, turbulent flows that favored native fish. Riparian vegetation exploded. As Schmidt wrote in a recent paper, the river used to resemble, well, a river, responding to seasons, precipitation, and snowmelt. But now it’s an institutionalized river, shaped less by nature than by rules and hydropower regulation.

Not everything suffered after the dam went up. Reservoir recreation exploded. Commercial river runners benefited from predictable year-round flows that let them run enormous rigs—the Cadillacs of the Colorado—through the canyon. Trout guides like Foster built booming businesses in the tailwater below the dam. But the losses were immense. Beaches eroded. Native fish collapsed. Indigenous burial grounds and archaeological sites disappeared beneath the reservoir. People think of the Grand Canyon as a natural wonderland. In fact, Schmidt said, it is closer to a “scenic ditch,” a utilitarian if sublime canal connecting two of creation’s most damaging, defended, and defamed reservoirs. “The nice words I could use,” Schmidt said, “are ‘It’s a completely novel ecosystem.’ If I don’t want to be nice, I can say, ‘It’s a completely screwed-up ecosystem.’” What Schmidt means is that the Colorado River below the dam is not a degraded version of the old river. It is something fundamentally new, a habitat produced by infrastructural demands, compromise, neglect, and relentless human intervention.

For years, Schmidt hoped that the answer to both the river’s and chub’s woes was better science. This belief was based on restoration as an article of faith: that the past is at least partly recoverable and that damage can be reversed if we are bold enough. But in practice, Schmidt realized that conservation on the Colorado has become less about restoring nature than about tending a patient on life support, every operation begetting a new set of complications. “This is a Rube Goldberg mess that we have made,” Schmidt said. “We’ve created such a morass of competing conflicts.” The result is that the river below the dam is now managed around a series of mutually incompatible desires: Cold water benefits the nonnative trout fishery and suppresses warmwater predators like smallmouth bass. But native fish like the chub evolved in a warmer river. In a pre-dam Colorado, Schmidt explained, warmer water would trigger spawning and help the chub thrive. The problem, again, is that warm water also favors the spread of the competitive smallmouth bass, who fall through the outlet tubes of the lowering reservoirs. All this means that the humpback chub’s best bet for survival now is to keep the river artificial, with a dam that keeps smallmouth bass at bay and water cold enough to nip these predators’ reproduction in the bud.

These environmental shifts have scrambled the old political alliances in the canyon. For decades, native-fish advocates fought against dam operators fixated on delivering massive amounts of water to cities and farms downstream, hydropower interests within the Bureau of Reclamation that use the Glen Canyon Dam like a cash register and sell its power to fund its other functions, and sport fishermen who celebrated the dam’s tailwater and the cold, brimming reservoir behind it. But now, as climate change lowers Lake Powell, these erstwhile opponents have converged. Suddenly, the people who protect the humpback chub and the people who protect trout want the same thing as the hydropower interests and the upper basin states, which is a relatively full reservoir at Lake Powell. This has produced what Schmidt calls “an odd, unholy alliance between people who want as much water in Powell as possible for water supply or electricity, and people who are focused on maintaining the novel ecosystem.” A few old-school river rats and environmental groups persist in the dream of taking down the dam and letting the native system and its native fish return to their former glory. But for the fish advocates who work with the necessary evil that is the dam, it’s a different story, and the hippies are now in bed with the power plant guys.

The irony would be funny if it weren’t so bleak. The chub—once nearly destroyed by the Glen Canyon Dam—is now utterly dependent on the dam’s continued existence. If the river returned to a warmer, more natural condition, reservoir fish would pour downstream and likely devastate the chub population. And if environmentalists succeeded in getting the dam taken down, the fish everyone is ostensibly trying to save might collapse alongside the novel ecosystem created by the dam. The modern Colorado, Schmidt explained, is now made up of relics and artifacts, remnants of the old river hanging on inside an entirely new one. And there is no way to protect both in the long run. This has produced two competing conservation philosophies in the canyon. The dominant paradigm—embraced by most federal agencies and major environmental NGOs—accepts that the dam is here to stay. “The dominant view is we can’t ever go back,” Schmidt said. “We have to deal with the situation at hand.” Under this framework, managers and scientists like Larry Stevens try to maintain the novel ecosystem while optimizing conditions for the humpback chub. But Schmidt belongs to what he calls the minority view. “I would like us to stop this unrelenting effort to hold on to an artificial river and keep making it even more artificial,” he said. He questions the need for the dam, the management program, and the fixation on saving the chub. In short, Schmidt’s philosophy defies the “sacred fish” approach of conservation—and makes him a heretic.

Lately, Schmidt has begun to imagine a bold and controversial solution. “I do not think the highest and best use of the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon is as a native fish aquarium,” said Schmidt. Instead of organizing the entire river around the fate of a single endangered species, Schmidt believes that managers should focus on restoring the river’s temperatures and temperaments, its ebbs and flows. The highest and best use of the river is for the river to be a river again. That could mean drilling bypass tunnels around the dam so that water could circumvent the reservoir and run downstream. It could mean letting the river warm again, diverting water around the dam, or even taking down the dam completely.

The humpback chub doesn’t deserve to pay for our human mistakes with extinction.

Schmidt is honest about the consequences. Under any of these approaches, the canyon would become rougher, warmer, and less predictable. The trout fishery would collapse, river-running economies would be forced to adapt, and the rebuilt beaches would erode again in uncontrolled floods. Lake Mead could fill to the top with sediment, threatening water deliveries to major American cities, and the upper basin states would have nowhere to hoard water in what is increasingly a zero-sum fight with the lower basin over water rights. The humpback chub might disappear altogether. But, in exchange, the river would become more alive.

Stevens, chief among the chub worshippers, is opposed. He’s spent half a century studying the Colorado River ecosystem, and given his song about setting the river free for the chub, you might assume he wants the dam gone and the Colorado restored to something wild and prelapsarian. But not anymore. “Taking out the dam would be a terrible mistake,” he told me flatly over the phone. Dropping reservoir levels have already unleashed a wave of new ecological threats, he explained. Warmwater invasive fish are moving downstream. Fish diseases are spreading. The dam, for all its destruction, has also kept some of the basin’s most aggressive predators out of the Grand Canyon for sixty years. “If you open the gates,” Stevens said, “all kinds of unforeseen and unpredictable damage” could follow.

This is the strange bind of the novel ecosystem: The dam destroyed the original river, but removing or bypassing it now might destroy what remains. Stevens is particularly fretful at the prospect of smallmouth bass, walleye, and other predatory nonnatives erupting through the canyon if the river warms too much. “These are species that, if their populations erupt in the Grand Canyon, will eliminate the native fish,” he said. Where Schmidt sees the possibility of a living river, Stevens sees ecocide. In forest conservation, he explained, there’s the concept of the silent forest. You can bring back all the stands of trees you want, but if you don’t bring back the conditions that support the creatures that live there—and sing and scuttle—it’s no forest at all, really.

Then there’s the matter of sacrificing the chub to save the river itself. For Stevens, extinction carries a different moral weight than any management could. “When we lose species, they’re gone forever,” he said. “That’s a permanent change, whereas the management of the river is something that can evolve over time.” Stevens pointed out that the Grand Canyon has already lost otters, fish, predators, parasites, and scavengers. The humpback chub does not merely need water. It needs these other species back, along with the food webs, spawning grounds, mud, insects, and seasonal cues that make the river a river. On the flip side, once an ecosystem begins unraveling, individual species become harder and harder to save in isolation.

What Stevens fears is not just extinction but emptiness: a river cosmetically restored but hollowed out in function, with warm muddy water moving through the canyon untroubled by the life it once nurtured. The Colorado is an ecosystem built atop another ecosystem built atop another ecosystem, each layer dependent on the next. Pull one thread loose and whole worlds come with it. And so Stevens putters away inside the machine. More monitoring. More negotiations. More thermal curtains and fish barriers and predator-suppression campaigns. More attempts to keep the reservoir full, lest the whole arrangement collapse outright. To Stevens’s mind, the river may no longer have a natural state to return to. His task now is simply to keep it as alive as possible.

A big part of me agrees with Stevens. The humpback chub doesn’t deserve to pay for our human mistakes with extinction. But Schmidt’s point is that the chub will suffer regardless of what we do—precisely because of what we have done already. And after months on and off the river, searching for, defending, and trying to understand this threatened animal, I increasingly believe that the fish has become a bureaucratic alibi for preserving the system as it stands. The thinking seems to be that if you save the chub, then you can’t question the dam, the reservoir it props up, the hydropower we sell to cities, or the entire illusion of endless growth and extraction that endangered the chub in the first place. Damage control makes us feudal vassals working our little fiefdoms of care. Conservation, in this sense, has been recruited to both manage and ultimately perpetuate the consequences of the dam. But if that doesn’t convince you, this might: Schmidt’s own research shows that, with climate change and overuse, the reservoirs could fail for good as early as this year. “The first opportunity is given to us by a warming planet,” Schmidt said. “Our hand is going to be forced.” In other words, Stevens’s worst fears are on the docket whether we like them or not. The question is no longer whether the Colorado River system will fundamentally change but how chaotic the transition will be when it comes—and what will be left of it afterward.

A billion dollars has been spent trying to rescue a river that is collapsing. I don’t want to lose the chub any more than, say, Foster wants to lose his trout, 35 percent of which have gone belly up because of a warming river and bureaucratic neglect. But the more I talk to people, the more obvious it seems that there is no saving the chub under the current system. We are managing a ruined river rather than confronting the political and infrastructural choices that ruined it. In doing so, we’re reproducing the very logic that caused the crisis. We have drunk deep from the well of technocratic liberalism, and now we are down to its last drops. If we stop intervening, a lot of people, animals, and ecosystems will suffer. But if we continue, the violence will be worse in the long run. All acts of restoration contend with a similar dilemma. The past is gone, and by trying to recreate it, we create an environment we don’t recognize and a future we can no longer control. A river we lose the more we seek it, a fish who might disappear because of our attempts to save it. “We move mountains to protect the humpback chub,” Foster told me. “Where does that stop? What’s the endgame?”

This is a conundrum not just for the Colorado but for every climate-ravaged corner of the globe, as we attempt to undo the damage we’ve done to the planet while refusing to undo the violence we’ve come to depend on. Modern conservation has spent decades managing fragments of life inside systems we broke long ago. We protect a coral reef from the ocean warming around it, relocate species northward as their climates shift beyond recognition. Patches of ancient forests survive as islands ringed by development. But this is a grievous error. Because the humpback chub is not merely its body or its fins or its hump; nor is it, simply, a species. As Stevens rightly observed, the humpback chub is the muddy, warm, treacherous river that made it. It is the canyon, the temperature, the velocity, and the chaos. It is the river itself, indistinguishable from the world that produced it. But sometimes, to save that world, we must contend with harming one of its inhabitants. There’s no good answer, and no one wants to do it. And yet we must choose.

Every system eventually produces its sacred objects—things so politically or morally untouchable that questioning them becomes sacrilege. Protection can be a form of violence, and great damage can be done in the name of devotion. The Colorado River is now governed by sacred fish and sacred dams. The humpback chub must be protected, even if that protection traps it inside an increasingly artificial river that requires constant shocking, tagging, poisoning, temperature manipulation, and intervention. The economically and environmentally central dam remains equally untouchable, even as the reservoirs shrink and the system fails around it. Conservation, in this modern sense, means being trapped between sacred objects, endlessly optimizing their mutual decline. The tragedy is not just that we ruined the river. It is that we keep mistaking management for salvation. Meanwhile the barons of water and power that benefit from calling the chub sacred continue to reign unquestioned, asking the river—and everything inside it—to endure a little longer.
